edition.title: Slow Burn - Sunday 25 October 2026
edition.fact: Edition 20. Three banks deliver, the Gulf bristles. Sunday 25 October 2026, the deep edition: Iran's army chief threatens US warships, the IRGC claims mines have hit tankers, and the Houthis hit Riyadh again, with Brent closed at $116.72; Kotak Mahindra Bank, AU Small Finance Bank and IDFC First Bank all grow profit sharply; SEBI's chairman lays out a four-part market road map - its bond pilot already live, its AI rules past consultation; Jio Platforms allotments land Monday ahead of Wednesday's listing; and fresh AI model claims from Kimi and Block, vendor labels attached.
edition.intro: The 5-minute lead route is first; sections carry the detail. This is the deep edition: the week's two stories - the oil premium and the results season - met on Saturday, and Monday's open is where they get priced. The long read goes inside SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey's to-do list for India's market plumbing.

concept.label: One concept a day
concept.name: Lottery demand
concept.line: When demand concentrates in the cheapest, most skewed ticket on the shelf, read it as entertainment spending, not conviction - and size your own ticket accordingly.

blocks.html: The Gulf, a hair-trigger weekend: Iran's armed forces chief says the US Navy cannot re-enter the Gulf and will be targeted if it tries; President Trump says a strike could come "maybe tomorrow" - or a "big, beautiful" deal; the IRGC claims mines have hit more tankers as missiles keep hitting Saudi targets. Brent closed Friday at $116.72, its highest since April.
Kotak Mahindra Bank: standalone profit up 29% year on year to Rs 4,212 crore, net interest income up 16% - but the margin slipped to 4.31% on bulk-deposit dilution.
AU Small Finance Bank: profit up 53% to Rs 858 crore, margin up 33 basis points year on year to 5.8%, bad loans down to 1.99%.
IDFC First Bank: profit up 196.5% to Rs 1,045 crore - against a Rs 352 crore year-ago base.

SEBI's road map: tokenised corporate bonds under "Demat 2.0" - a pilot already live, secondary trading next - a short-selling review, graded broker compliance and responsible-AI guidelines being finalised.

Jio, the eve of allotment: BSE's own final demand schedule shows the issue 9.73 times subscribed on its platform, retail barely crossing full cover while institutions bid 33 times. Allotment Monday, listing Wednesday.
AI race: Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro - a 3-trillion-class open-weight model with weights promised by 4 November - and Block's Dessa, a voice model trained only on speech. Vendor claims, labelled.
Monday's setup: oil on a knife edge, three bank prints to price, an Infosys guidance cut to digest, the Fed Wednesday and Jio's listing the same morning. The editor's read.

blocks.title: Iran's army chief threatens US warships; Trump muses about 'another Epic Fury'

blocks.html: The war's rhetoric escalated on Saturday even as its front lines stayed roughly where Friday left them. Ali Abdollahi, chief of general staff of Iran's armed forces, said the US Navy is incapable of re-entering the Gulf or its periphery because Iran can target any vessel in the region: "The US president can only dream of their soldiers and military again entering the Persian Gulf. They will take this wish to the grave," he said in a statement carried by state media. President Trump, at a Florida rally on Friday, said the US military "may do another Epic Fury" - his name for the bombing campaign that opened the war - and framed the choice as fresh strikes or continued blockade-and-sanctions pressure (Al Jazeera's Tehran dispatch, 24 October).

The on-the-water picture: the IRGC - Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the parallel military that runs the naval harassment campaign - said seven tankers were attacked or hit mines overnight into Thursday, and claimed two supertankers struck mines on Friday; vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf chokepoint that carried about 21% of global petroleum liquids consumption in 2022, the US Energy Information Administration's count, keep coming under attack. The Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen hit Riyadh again on Saturday, with Dammam's airport and the Shaybah oilfield targeted in recent days; Saudi forces bombed Marib, Taiz and other Houthi-held provinces. Washington has reportedly ordered many diplomatic staff out of Saudi Arabia. The diplomacy: Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt met the UK, France, Germany and Italy in Istanbul on Friday - no US, no Iran - and Turkiye's foreign minister Hakan Fidan said afterwards that "a new attack on Iran would widen the war". Separately, Axios reported on Saturday that US intelligence sees Iran having "substantially increased" efforts to strike American officials. Claims by state-linked Iranian media that Tehran has activated a "dead hand" retaliation doctrine are just that - claims - but they show the direction of the signalling. On Saturday, Trump sharpened the timing himself: asked how far along his thinking on an attack was, he said "We're thinking about doing it, and maybe tomorrow" - Sunday - while holding out a deal track: "I may have to finish it off, or maybe they'll make a deal... Either way, we win." He also claimed oil shipments through Hormuz have risen above pre-war levels, without offering figures (Anadolu Agency, 24 October). Brent settled Friday at $116.72, its highest since April; US WTI at $103.27 (CNBC; Al Jazeera).

Why it matters to you: for the insurance desk, an active war-risk theatre in the Gulf reprices marine and aviation cover and reinsurance renewals across the region - and every $1 on crude adds up to $2 billion a year to India's import bill (Indian Express's arithmetic on PPAC data). Two elections frame the next ten days: Israel votes on Tuesday and the US midterms land on 3 November, and both capitals are campaigning on Iran.

Editor's takeaway: the weekend produced louder threats, more mine claims and a president naming Sunday as a possible strike day while floating a deal - the premium is still paying for the strike that has not happened, and the window Trump named is today.
Source: Al Jazeera, Tehran, 24 Oct (read in full) / Anadolu Agency, 24 Oct (read in full) / CNBC oil wrap, 23 Oct

blocks.title: Saturday's bank results: three sharp profit rises, one margin question

blocks.html: Three banks reported on Saturday, and the headline numbers all rose sharply. Kotak Mahindra Bank earned Rs 4,212 crore standalone in the September quarter, up 29% on the Rs 3,253 crore of a year ago, with net interest income (NII, the gap between what a bank earns on loans and pays on deposits) up 16% to Rs 8,459 crore; consolidated profit rose 26% to Rs 5,645 crore. AU Small Finance Bank earned Rs 858 crore, up 53% on Rs 561 crore, with NII up 32% to Rs 2,820 crore, gross bad loans down to 1.99% of the book from 2.41%, deposits up 28.6% to Rs 1,70,460 crore and advances up 27.9% to Rs 1,50,291 crore. IDFC First Bank earned Rs 1,045 crore standalone, up 196.5% - against a depressed Rs 352 crore year-ago quarter - with NII up 21% to Rs 6,184 crore; consolidated profit was Rs 1,049 crore. All figures from the banks' own exchange-filed releases and presentations.

The margin line is where the three diverge, and it is the line Monday will trade. Kotak's net interest margin (NIM - NII as a share of earning assets) fell to 4.31% from 4.53% in the June quarter and 4.54% a year ago; the bank attributes the moderation to its FCNR(B) bulk-deposit mobilisation during the quarter - cheap-rate-window foreign-currency deposits that dilute margin while adding low-cost funding. AU went the other way: NIM up 33 basis points year on year to 5.8% (a basis point is a hundredth of a percentage point). IDFC First's release flags the same FCNR dilution optics while noting the funding should benefit profit and return ratios. The cross-bank read this results season: deposit cost, not loan growth, is deciding who gets paid - J&K Bank fell 16% on Friday on exactly this line, its margin down to 3.17%.

Why it matters to you: margins are the transmission from Friday's oil spike and the 94.93 rupee to your world: if funding costs stay high, lenders protect margin by re-pricing loans and by pushing fee lines - including insurance distribution. Monday's reaction in these three stocks is the market's verdict on whether profit growth with a smaller margin still gets paid.

Editor's takeaway: AU printed the complete quarter - growth, margin and asset quality all moving the right way; Kotak printed the biggest profit with the one question attached; IDFC First's near-tripling is real cash in the bank, off a low base.
Source: AU Small Finance Bank press release on BSE (primary) / IDFC First Bank press release on BSE (primary) / Kotak results release on BSE (primary)

blocks.title: SEBI's chairman draws the next market map: tokenised bonds, a short-selling review, AI rules

blocks.html: SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey used ANMI's International Capital Market Convention - the broking industry's own gathering - to lay out a road map he framed in four parts - simpler rules, deeper markets, responsible technology and wider access - across about a dozen items; four of them change the market's plumbing most. First, "Demat 2.0": tokenised corporate bonds - already live as a pilot since 10 September, with three issuers raising Rs 1,025 crore settled against the RBI's wholesale CBDC, per the launch release - and the speech puts secondary trading as the next phase, the launch release naming the path: the existing RFQ platforms, then retail access, aimed at a corporate-bond market that now has about Rs 61 lakh crore outstanding but stays institution-to-institution. Second, a review of short-selling and the stock lending and borrowing (SLB) mechanism - the rules that govern betting against stocks. Third, a graded compliance framework for brokers - obligations scaled to an intermediary's scale, client exposure and technology reliance. Fourth, an AI agenda: responsible-AI guidelines now being finalised after a June 2025 consultation - tiered obligations, kill switches, aligned with IOSCO, the global securities-regulators' body - plus an AI sandbox SEBI says it is exploring. He also flagged easier NRI onboarding. The four are at different stations: the bond pilot is live, the AI guidelines are past consultation, and the review and the grading are exploratory - no circulars yet (speech text, read in full; pilot figures and phasing from the 10 September launch release).

Why it matters to you: if tokenised bonds arrive with real secondary trading, a retail saver gets a third asset between fixed deposits and equity - and insurers get a deeper bond market to match liabilities against. The short-selling review is the one your watch list cares about: SLB reform changes how cheaply crowded longs can be hedged.

Editor's takeaway: treat this as a progress report, not a rulebook - the tells are dated documents: RFQ secondary trading going live for the bonds, the final AI guidelines, and consultation papers on the other two over the next board cycles.
Source: Speech text, SEBI website (primary, read in full) / Speech page / Demat 2.0 pilot launch release, 10 Sep (owning)

blocks.title: Jio Platforms: allotment Monday, the owning numbers behind the record

blocks.html: Jio Platforms' Rs 30,213 crore all-fresh issue - India's largest IPO - closed Friday, and the official record is BSE's final demand schedule, timestamped 6:58 PM Friday: the issue was bid 9.73 times on BSE's platform, with institutions (QIBs - qualified institutional buyers, the mutual funds and foreign funds) at 33.33 times, non-institutional bidders at 4.09 times, retail at 1.01 times, employees at 1.05 times and Reliance shareholders at 2.23 times; 192.27 crore shares were bid against 19.75 crore on offer, in a Rs 1,065-1,119 band with a Rs 54 employee discount and a 12-share lot. The anchor book placed on 19 October raised Rs 8,110 crore ahead of the public issue; the registrar is Kfin Technologies and the allotment is expected Monday 26 October, with listing on BSE and NSE on Wednesday 28 October. At the Rs 1,119 cap, Jio is valued at about Rs 10.3 lakh crore.

Why it matters to you: retail barely crossed full cover at 1.01 times on the BSE platform - one exchange slice of the book - and Monday's allotment is the first hard answer. Wednesday's listing lands the same morning as the Fed decision: the market's verdict on a Rs 10.3 lakh crore tariff-hike story will arrive on a noisy day.
Editor's takeaway: the demand story was institutional conviction against retail caution - Wednesday's open prices which book was right.
Source: BSE final demand schedule (official) / BSE issue page (official)

blocks.title: AI race: a 3-trillion-class open model and a voice model trained only on speech

blocks.html: Moonshot AI - the Beijing lab behind the Kimi assistant - announced Kimi K3.1 Pro on its blog: a roughly 3-trillion-parameter-class open-weight model with a 1-million-token context window (about seven novels of input at once) and a "Highspeed" mode it says runs 2-3 times faster, with model weights promised by 4 November. The benchmark table on the page is vendor-run: what would count as verification is the public weights plus independent evaluations. Jack Dorsey's Block published Dessa: a conversation model it says was trained only on human speech - no text pretraining, no borrowed language model - and which holds full-duplex conversations (it can listen and talk at the same time, like a person). Block calls it a world first; that is a vendor claim, and what would count as verification is third-party demos and latency tests.

Why it matters to you: open weights at the frontier keep compressing what a side project can do for free - if K3.1 Pro's weights land on 4 November, a coding or analysis agent you self-host gets materially better that week. A speech-native model is the other end of the same trend: interfaces moving from typing to talking.

Editor's takeaway: both sets of capability claims stay vendor-labelled until third parties test them outside the makers' own pages - the date to hold is 4 November, when Kimi says the open weights arrive; for Dessa, Block promises more recordings on X.
Source: Kimi blog (vendor, read in full) / Block Dessa page (vendor, read in full)

groups.heading: Markets: the week that priced a strike

blocks.html: Friday's closes, the last prints before this weekend's escalation: the Dow fell 652.82 points (1.23%) to 52,215.16, the S&P 500 lost 0.52% to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq 0.21% to 25,955.34, as US crude topped $100 and the selloff broadened out of tech into staples, utilities and healthcare; on the week the S&P lost 0.5%, the Nasdaq 0.7%, the Dow gained 0.4% (CNBC's post-close wrap; AP's levels). The VIX - Wall Street's fear gauge, the price of S&P options - crossed 20 intraday on Thursday and again on Friday, touching 20.66, but settled Friday at 19.45, below last Friday's 19.99: the first weekly close above 20 since June that CNBC had on track did not materialize at the official close (CBOE's official daily data). American Express fell more than 3% after saying it would cut about 5% of its workforce to "prepare for AI". In India: the Sensex slipped 126 points to 73,124, the Nifty 88 to 22,600, but the midcap index plunged 2.2% and the Bank Nifty 1.2%, with six declines for every advance (CNBC-TV18); BSE's own snapshot shows the Bankex down 1.10% and its IT index down 0.66%. Foreign investors were net buyers of Rs 887.65 crore and domestic institutions of Rs 3,235.36 crore (provisional exchange data) - the fall came despite institutional buying on both sides. The rupee fell 12 paise to a provisional 94.93 per dollar (PTI via The Hindu). Gold, the paradox of the week, dipped under $4,000 an ounce intraday for the first time since mid-July - as higher energy prices fuel inflation concerns and reinforce elevated US rate expectations, which is poison for a metal that pays nothing; traders see a 92% chance the Fed holds next week and a 78% probability of a December hike (CME FedWatch, cited by CNBC Friday).

The configuration into Monday: Brent at $116.72 after a weekend of threats but no new strike, three sets of bank results to price, an Infosys guidance cut to digest, the Fed's decision Wednesday and Jio's listing the same morning - with foreign investors, unusually, on the buy side.

groups.heading: SEBI's road map, item by item

blocks.html: Demat 2.0 and tokenised bonds. India's Rs 61-lakh-crore corporate-bond market is institution-to-institution: big tickets, thin trading. Demat 2.0 is already live as a pilot - SEBI launched it on 10 September, and three issuers (REC, L&T and IIFL) have raised Rs 1,025 crore in tokenised bonds settled against the RBI's wholesale CBDC, held in ordinary demat accounts. The speech puts secondary trading as the next phase; the launch release names the path - the existing RFQ platforms, then retail access - the bond-market equivalent of what dematerialisation did for shares.

Short-selling and SLB review. The stock lending and borrowing mechanism - the pipe through which shares are borrowed to sell short - has stayed thin in India while cash-and-carry and futures do most of the work. A review signals the regulator wants two-way markets that do not depend on derivatives alone.

Graded broker compliance. One rulebook today stretches from two-person brokerages to bank-owned giants; a graded framework would scale obligations to an intermediary's scale, client exposure and reliance on technology - the chairman's three factors. For the broking industry in the room at ANMI, this was the applause line.

AI: sandbox plus responsible-AI guidelines. The rulebook is not starting from zero - SEBI ran a consultation on responsible AI/ML in June 2025, and the final guidelines are now being finalised: tiered obligations by risk, kill switches, aligned with IOSCO. The newer idea is an AI sandbox the speech says SEBI is exploring, where tools can be tested safely. For any fintech shipping models into distribution or advice, this is the framework your compliance team will be quoting in a year.

The four sit at different stations: the bond pilot is already live, the AI guidelines are past consultation and being finalised, and the short-selling review and graded compliance are exploratory. The long read tells the story of the list itself - and what would prove it wrong.

blocks.title: The FCNR(B) ghost in Saturday's margins

blocks.html: Two of Saturday's three banks flagged the same accounting ghost: deposits raised through RBI's FCNR(B) swap window - the concessional facility, closed 31 August, that let banks bring in foreign-currency non-resident deposits cheaply. Kotak's margin fell to 4.31% "largely on account of FCNR(B) mobilisation during the quarter"; IDFC First's release calls the same effect "optically NIM-dilutive" while arguing the funding benefits profit, earnings per share and return on equity. The mechanism: the window's swap pricing made these deposits cheap in all-in cost, but the balance-sheet swelling they cause dilutes the margin ratio even when the money is profitable. So the same deposits can be good for profit and bad for the margin print - which is why Monday's analysts will ask both banks for the ex-FCNR margin before they re-rate anything.

Why it matters to you: when a bank's margin "misses" on a deliberate, profitable funding trade, the correct read is the adjusted margin, not the reported one - the same lesson the deposit-growth headlines taught earlier this season.
Source: AU press release (primary) / IDFC First press release (primary)

The insight - retail demand is not one thing: BSE's final schedule for Jio shows retail at 1.01 times cover while QIBs bid 33.33 times. Read plainly, that is not "retail loves IPOs" or "retail is scared"; it is retail demand thinning out precisely when the issue is large and the valuation debate is real. For a founder, the lesson cuts both ways: a giant issue needs institutional conviction to price, while a small issue can ride lottery demand it should not mistake for a verdict on the business.

One startup idea - the allotment-odds desk: a free tool that converts each open IPO's live exchange subscription data (category-wise, like the BSE schedule above) into plain-English allotment odds for a retail applicant, updated twice a day during the issue window, with an archive of how odds related to listing outcomes. Who pays: brokers and IPO-advisory newsletters, for the API and the white-label widget; the consumer page is the funnel. Why now: Jio just put a crore-plus applications through the system and allotment anxiety is the week's dominant retail emotion. First step: build the category-odds calculator for the three issues open this month and publish the method note.

blocks.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro: open weights at the frontier, if 4 November delivers

blocks.html: Moonshot AI's blog post announces Kimi K3.1 Pro as a roughly 3-trillion-parameter-class open-weight model: a 1-million-token context window, a "Highspeed" mode the post says runs 2-3 times faster, and benchmark tables showing it competitive with the top proprietary models. Every performance number on that page is vendor-run; the verification path is explicit - weights by 4 November, then independent evaluators can check. If the weights land, this is the strongest open-weight option yet for long-document work: roughly seven lakh words fit in one context.
Source: Kimi blog (vendor, read in full)

blocks.title: Block's Dessa: a voice model with no text inside

blocks.html: Every voice assistant you have used is a text model wearing a headset: speech in, transcribed to text, answered by a language model, synthesised back. Block says Dessa removes the text entirely - trained only on human conversation, holding full-duplex calls where it can be interrupted and talks over you back. The claim is Block's own, with no third-party test yet; what would count: an independent side-by-side against the big voice modes on interruption handling and latency. If the approach holds, it changes what phone-first products - insurance renewals, claims intake - can feel like in two years.
Source: Block Dessa page (vendor, read in full)
Radar note: X was not accessible from our side for this edition; the radar above is built from vendor pages read in full, with vendor claims labelled.

K3.1 Pro's practical meaning for your stack, if the 4 November weights arrive as promised: a 1M-token context changes how you build tools more than another point on a benchmark does. Whole-repo analysis stops needing a retrieval layer; your codebase, its tests and its docs fit in one prompt. The test on release day: point it at your messiest repository and ask for a dependency-ordered refactor plan - if it holds the whole repo without dropping files, the open-weight stack just caught the hosted one for your workload. Until independent runs exist, treat the benchmark table as a brochure; the verified facts today are the licence promise (open weights), the context length and the date.

Listen to a voice-native AI (about 15 minutes). Block's Dessa page (linked in AI Race) does not offer a live demo - it hosts recordings of real conversations, including one where Dessa talks to another AI. Play three of them on your phone with a skeptic's ear: (1) the interruption handling - Dessa gets talked over and recovers the thread, the thing text-based voice modes fumble; (2) the emotional register - Block claims it hears sarcasm and a voice cracking, so test whether you can tell; (3) the knowledge question - Block says every fact Dessa knows came from raw sound, so ask how much it can reliably know. The point: these are curated vendor recordings, not independent tests - your ear is the only check available until third parties get access, and knowing the difference between a demo reel and a demo is the skill. Time: 15 minutes.

In 2009, Alok Kumar of the University of Texas at Austin published a study in the Journal of Finance with a title that asks its own question: "Who Gambles in the Stock Market?". His finding, from US investor data: the propensity to gamble and investment decisions are correlated. Individual investors systematically prefer stocks with lottery features - cheap tickets, skewed payoffs, long-shot upside - and the demand behaves like lottery demand: it rises in economic downturns, it is stronger where state lotteries are popular, and it concentrates among lower-income investors, who consequently underperform the most. Lotteries and lottery stocks, he showed, attract the same clienteles.

Watch the concept at work in this week's IPO tape, on the exchange's own record: Jio Platforms - India's largest issue at Rs 30,213 crore - drew retail cover of just 1.01 times on BSE's platform while institutions bid 33.33 times, with 192.27 crore shares bid against 19.75 crore on offer (BSE's final demand schedule). The retail rupee stayed cautious on the biggest business of the year. A subscription multiple describes the ticket's shape and the bidder mix - small tickets and skewed-looking payoffs are what pull lottery demand - never the business's quality. "The IPO was subscribed 100 times" is a statement about the structure of demand, not about what a company is worth.

The applications reach your desk. In insurance product work, the same preference is why low-premium, high-payout-framed products outsell actuarially superior boring ones - the customer is buying the ticket shape, not the expected value. In markets, a stock's retail following growing on "multi-bagger" chatter is lottery demand arriving, not analysis. In your own allocation, the honest question when a small cheap ticket excites you is whether you are investing or buying a lottery with extra steps.
The decision rule: when demand concentrates in the cheapest, most skewed ticket on the shelf, read it as entertainment spending, not conviction - and size your own ticket accordingly.

Sixty-second recall: close the page and answer: (1) What did Kumar's 2009 study show? (2) When does lottery-type demand rise? (3) Which investors overweight lottery stocks most, and with what result? (4) The decision rule, in one sentence. Answers: (1) gambling propensity and investment decisions are correlated - individuals prefer lottery-feature stocks. (2) in economic downturns, and where state lotteries are popular. (3) lower-income investors, who underperform the most as a result. (4) demand concentrated in cheap, skewed tickets is entertainment, not conviction - size your ticket accordingly.

groups.heading: Term of the day: anchor investor

blocks.html: An institutional investor allotted shares in an IPO ahead of the public issue opening, at the final price, with a lock-in - 30 days on part of the allotment, 90 on the rest - so it cannot flip on listing day. The book-build's signal fire: a strong anchor book tells later bidders that big money has already committed at the price. Jio Platforms' anchor round, placed on 19 October, raised Rs 8,110 crore ahead of the public issue (BSE's issue page carries the anchor-allocation notice). The term to not confuse it with: cornerstone investors in global listings play a similar role but typically carry longer lock-ins.

Research, not advice. This is the standing board into Monday, printed in full: one qualified setup, five watchlist names with named triggers, three left out with reasons. The frame is five setup slots plus five on watch, and empty slots stay empty rather than forcing picks. No orders are placed by this desk; every call is scored in the standing ledger. No Saturday session means no new price data - these are Friday's levels.

The one qualified setup - HCL Technologies. A conditional entry at Rs 1,351-1,378 (the post-results shelf), stop Rs 1,346.90, target Rs 1,466.80 (the adjusted 20-session high); risk-reward about 1:2.4-2.5 net of verified costs at the worst permitted fill of 1,378. It activates only if price trades into the zone with no prior-day trade at or below the stop first; if the zone and the stop first trade on the same day, the order is unknowable from daily data and conservative scoring assumes the worst fill, then the stop. Validity lapses untriggered after Friday 30 October. Infosys's Friday-night guidance cut is precisely the scenario that could fill it at Monday's open - or gap it away.

On watch, triggers named, none a setup yet. ONGC (Rs 226.00) - a three-week coil inside 218.50-238.75 with crude as the driver; the trigger is a breakout above 228 with crude holding, but at that fill a structural stop yields only about 1:1.76, below the screen, so it waits. JSW Steel (Rs 1,187.00) - a record Q2 at the owning release; the trigger is holding 1,158.95, then reclaiming 1,218.90-1,222.30; the risk-reward screens at about 1:1.2, and the promoter pledge rose to 12.25% of the promoter holding in the September quarter (BSE shareholding data). Infosys (Rs 1,154.50) - the trigger is deliberately qualitative: how Monday prices Friday's FY27 guidance cut to 1-2%; Friday's flash print is excluded from structure. Tech Mahindra (Rs 1,789.40) - the trigger is a reclaim of 1,845.95, Friday's high; the recommended 1:1 bonus still has no record date. Kotak Mahindra Bank (Rs 430.10) - Saturday's profit growth with the margin question attached: strength above Rs 437.55 keeps it live, weakness below Rs 420 shelves it, and Monday's reaction is the test.

Left out, with reasons. TCS - up 22% in October and above the only published broker target, so there is no honest risk-reward structure at Rs 2,528. Shriram Finance - a day-one post-results breakdown, with the 833.65-915.50 range unresolved. Wipro - the weakest verified fundamentals of the large-cap IT pack, bookings down 22.9% QoQ in its own release.

What a trade costs. About 0.224% round trip in verified statutory charges on a BSE delivery trade, before brokerage; the worked HCLTech example nets about +Rs 8,546 against -Rs 3,432 per 100 shares at the worst permitted fill. Every level above is reconciled from the official BSE bhavcopy, and the full scoring rules and outcome log live in the standing ledger: Slow Burn swing research, 24 October.

What I think the market is missing - an analytical read, not advice. Saturday's three bank results land on a market that spent Friday punishing margins, and I expect it to sort them by margin direction, not by profit growth: AU gets paid first (growth and asset quality moving right; margin up 33 basis points on last year at 5.8%, a shade below the June quarter's 5.9%), Kotak gets paid with a question mark (the 4.31% NIM is FCNR-diluted, and Monday's call will be about the ex-FCNR number), and IDFC First's 196.5% gets discounted for its Rs 352-crore base - and profit is also off the June quarter's Rs 1,075 crore. My falsifiable marker: if IDFC First outperforms both Kotak and AU on Monday, the market is trading optics over margin mechanics and this read is wrong. On oil: the weekend added threats, mine claims and Trump's own Sunday strike window, but no new US strike as this goes to press - I expect the premium to hold rather than spike at Monday's reopen, wrong if Brent gaps above $120, which was already the marker from Saturday's edition.

Scoreboard on Saturday's markers: one leg fired, one waits. I said the stabilisation read fails if Kotak reports a margin contraction with weaker guidance, or if Brent gaps above $120 before Monday. Kotak did report a margin contraction - 4.31% from 4.53% - but attributed to FCNR(B) mobilisation, and no weaker guidance accompanied it; the marker is strained, not broken. Brent never reopened over the weekend, so the second leg is untested. Honestly counted: the stabilisation call goes into Monday weakened.

items: Jio lists Wednesday, the same morning as the Fed decision. Watch the open against the Rs 1,119 cap and the Rs 10.3 lakh crore valuation: a strong debut pulls index money toward the RIL complex; a weak one lands on a day the Fed could sour everything anyway. Wrong if the Fed dominates so completely that the listing tracks the index instead of the book.

The December hike repricing: 78% priced as of Friday (CME FedWatch via CNBC). The chain runs oil to inflation to the Fed; Thursday's PCE report is the next hard input. Wrong if Brent gives back the week before Wednesday, deflating the inflation argument.

SEBI's road map: the bond pilot is already live and the AI guidelines are being finalised after consultation - the proof for the rest is dated paperwork: RFQ secondary trading going live for the bonds, the final AI guidelines, and consultation papers on the short-selling review and graded compliance. Wrong if none of the four produces a dated document over the next two board cycles; that reads as a speech, not a programme.

IRDAI's distribution-economics consultation: the listed comment window closes today, 25 October. Watch for an extension notice or, more telling, a summary of comments - the first look at how hard the industry is pushing back on the expense caps. Wrong if the deadline passes quietly with no extension and no summary; then the paper moves toward a final regulation on schedule.
Today, Sun 25 Oct: public comments close on IRDAI's distribution-economics consultation paper (listed deadline).
Mon 26 Oct: Jio Platforms allotment expected; first session to price Saturday's bank results and the Infosys guidance cut; US crude futures reopen after the weekend's threats.
Tue 27 Oct: Israel votes, with Iran policy at the centre (Al Jazeera); the Fed's two-day meeting begins (Federal Reserve calendar); L&T Technology Services Rs 20 dividend goes ex.
Wed 28 Oct: Jio Platforms lists on BSE and NSE; the Fed's decision and press conference; Nippon Life India AMC dividend record date.
Thu 29 Oct: US PCE inflation report - the Fed's preferred gauge, and the December repricing's next test.
Fri 30 Oct: the HCL Technologies swing setup's published validity lapses - the ledger scores it either way.
